summary.case_overview: In Justice K. S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (Writ Petition (Civil) No. 494 of 2012), a nine-judge Bench of the Supreme Court of India unanimously held that the right to privacy is a constitutionally protected fundamental right [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 430]. The Court declared that privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21, as well as an integral facet of the freedoms contained in Part III of the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 431]. In doing so, the Court expressly overruled the prior decisions in M. P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra (an eight-judge bench decision) and Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. (a six-judge bench decision) to the extent that they had held that privacy is not a fundamental right under the Indian Constitution [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 430] [Page 431].
summary.facts_of_case: The case arose out of a challenge to the Aadhaar scheme propounded by the Government of India, under which demographic and biometric data of residents were collected and compiled for various services and welfare benefits [Page 15]. The petitioners challenged the scheme on the ground that the compulsory collection and usage of personal demographic and biometric data infringed upon the fundamental Right to Privacy [Page 15]. During the proceedings, the Union of India, relying on the earlier larger-bench judgments in M. P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962), argued that no fundamental right to privacy exists under the Indian Constitution [Page 1] [Page 78] [Page 144]. Consequently, on July 18, 2017, a Constitution Bench referred the core question—whether the right to privacy is a fundamental right under the Indian Constitution—to a nine-judge Bench to examine the correctness of M. P. Sharma and Kharak Singh [Page 78].
summary.legal_issues:
1. Whether the right to privacy is a fundamental right protected under Part III of the Constitution of India, specifically under Article 21 and the freedoms guaranteed therein [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 78].
2. Whether the decisions in M. P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra and Kharak Singh v. State of U.P., which observed that privacy is not a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution, lay down the correct legal position [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 78].
3. What are the contours, facets, and limits of the right to privacy, and what standards must a law meet to justify an invasion into an individual's privacy [Page 3] [Page 6] [Page 277] [Page 424].
summary.important_arguments_or_content:
1. Union of India's Submissions: The Union argued that privacy is not a fundamental right under the Indian Constitution, relying on the binding precedents of M. P. Sharma (8 Judges) and Kharak Singh (6 Judges) [Page 78] [Page 144]. It was further contended that recognizing privacy as a constitutional fundamental right would require a constitutional amendment and cannot be created through judicial interpretation [Page 2] [Page 19].
2. Petitioners' Submissions: The petitioners argued that technological developments enable intrusion into a citizen's home and personal sphere without physical entry, making privacy an indispensable facet of personal liberty and human dignity [Page 412] [Page 428]. They asserted that privacy is a natural and inalienable right that inheres in human existence and must be protected against both State and non-State actors [Page 4] [Page 8] [Page 428].
3. M.P. Sharma Context: It was noted during arguments and analysis that M.P. Sharma pertained specifically to Article 20(3) and testimonial compulsion regarding search and seizure, without evaluating Article 21 or other fundamental freedoms [Page 1] [Page 5] [Page 354].
summary.court_reasoning:
1. Intrinsic Link to Life, Liberty, and Dignity: The Court reasoned that privacy is an essential condition for the exercise of personal liberty and human dignity under Article 21, as well as other Part III freedoms [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 7] [Page 15]. Living a life of dignity requires protecting the inner sphere of an individual's personality from unwanted State and private intrusions [Page 2] [Page 3] [Page 428].
2. Natural and Inalienable Rights: Life, personal liberty, and privacy are natural, primordial, and inalienable rights that exist prior to the Constitution; the Constitution recognizes and preserves them rather than bestowing them as state bounties [Page 4] [Page 8] [Page 15] [Page 166].
3. Re-examination of Precedents: The Court reasoned that M. P. Sharma did not rule on whether privacy could be derived from Article 21 or Part III [Page 1] [Page 5]. In Kharak Singh, while night domiciliary visits were struck down for violating ordered liberty, the second portion denying a guaranteed right to privacy was internally inconsistent and incorrect in law [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 5] [Page 6].
4. Facets and Modern Context: Privacy includes informational privacy, bodily integrity, decisional autonomy, sanctuary, and repose [Page 3] [Page 6] [Page 233] [Page 419]. In the modern digital age, informational privacy requires regulating data collection and usage by both State and non-State entities [Page 3] [Page 10] [Page 266] [Page 424].
5. Non-Absolute Nature and Test of Scrutiny: Privacy is not absolute [Page 3] [Page 6] [Page 277]. Any State interference must satisfy a three-fold test: (i) legality (existence of law); (ii) need (legitimate State aim, such as national security or crime prevention); and (iii) proportionality (a rational nexus between the object and the means used) [Page 3] [Page 277] [Page 424].
summary.decision_or_conclusion:
The nine-judge Bench answered the reference in the following terms:
1. The decision in M. P. Sharma, to the extent it holds that the right to privacy is not protected by the Constitution, stands overruled [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 430].
2. The decision in Kharak Singh, to the extent it holds that the right to privacy is not protected by the Constitution, stands overruled [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 430] [Page 431].
3. The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 431].
4. Decisions rendered after Kharak Singh which recognized the right to privacy lay down the correct position of law, and the batch of petitions was ordered to be sent back to the original three-judge Bench for adjudication on merits [Page 5] [Page 15] [Page 431].

summary.simplified_explanation: In simple terms, the Supreme Court of India was asked to decide whether Indian citizens have a fundamental right to privacy under the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 78]. The central government had argued that privacy was not a fundamental right based on old legal rulings from 1954 and 1962 [Page 1] [Page 78]. A special nine-judge Bench of the Supreme Court unanimously held that privacy IS a fundamental right [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 430]. The Court explained that privacy is a core part of personal liberty, human dignity, and personal choice under Article 21 of the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 7]. It protects people's personal information, home life, bodily decisions, and online activity from unlawful government or private intrusion [Page 3] [Page 10] [Page 419] [Page 428]. However, privacy is not absolute, and the government can restrict it only if there is a valid law, a legitimate reason (like national security or preventing crime), and the measure used is fair and proportionate [Page 3] [Page 277] [Page 424].
